<reason>Both sides argued competently, but B kept the debate anchored to the motion's actual line — banning source-based blanket exclusion while preserving individualized screening for ability-to-pay and documented conduct — and defended that distinction consistently under pressure. When A accused B of contradiction ("bounded" vs "real" burden), B's PQ answer and Rebuttal 2 (a manageable burden an owner still prefers to avoid) resolved the tension coherently; A never landed a clean self-contradiction. A's strongest late move was the "asymmetry" framing (mandates can only subtract supply via exit; incentives can only fail to add), introduced in Rebuttal 2 and pressed hard in closing. It was clever and rhetorically sharp, but A explicitly admitted never quantifying exit (A4.4) and asked the tie to break on directionality alone — a burden-shift B's closing partially exposed ("treating continued exclusion as costless") though without fully dismantling the framing. A's opening was also clipped for exceeding the word limit, a real execution cost that blunted its foundational case. On balance, B's tighter, more internally consistent handling of the discretion-vs-mandate scope question, plus cleaner responses to pressure, gives it a modest but clear edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 "asymmetry" argument (mandates can only subtract supply, incentives can only fail to add) versus B's closing reply that continued categorical exclusion is not a costless baseline — the most decisive exchange, only partially resolved, but B's framing of the actual proposition's screening/exclusion line held up better across the whole debate.</best_rebuttal>
